title: The River and the Lake

post.author: u/depot_tray_jozef
post.title: I'm the night clerk at a bus depot. Tonight's report says route 4 carried 1,904 passengers. Route 4 has one bus, and its slip in my tray says 952.

blocks.text: I'm Jozef, night clerk at the Burnhollow Buses depot: 45 buses, and me at the counter from 22:00 to 06:00. Every morning the company sends the council a claim, and the council pays a set amount for each passenger. Our rule is simple: one ticket is one passenger.

When a bus docks, it parks on its bay for the night and its ticket machine hands over the day. First the machine joins the depot's wifi. Then it sends the day's tickets, as one file, into the lake: a store on head office's computers that keeps raw files just as they came, like a sack of unopened post.

When the whole file is in, the bus has checked in, and a line appears on my screen: "bus 17 checked in, 952 tickets". Then the driver prints an end-of-day slip with the same count and drops it in my tray.

At 02:00 the nightly job runs: a set of instructions that head office's computers carry out once a night. A timer called cron starts it, like an alarm clock set for 02:00 every day. Head office's data team looks after the job. I only see what comes out.

It works in steps. First it reads every file in tonight's part of the lake. Then it cleans each one into rows, one line per ticket: route, bus, time, fare. Then it loads the rows into the warehouse: tidy tables, like spreadsheets, built for reports. Last, it counts each route's rows into the morning report.

Thursday 15 October. At 23:15 a lorry shed its load on the bridge road, and routes 7 and 12 were sent the long way round. Route 4's only bus, 17, docked at 23:40, and Marcelline dropped its slip in my tray: 952 tickets. By 00:50, 38 buses had checked in. At 02:00 the job ran. Route 7's four buses and route 12's three came in together at 02:20.

The runbook is our binder of what to do when. Its page for late buses says: "If buses are late, run the job again after they arrive." So at 02:40 I pressed run again. The job went through all its steps a second time, over every file in tonight's part of the lake: all 45. I did the same on snowy nights last winter, and the reports came out right. Since then, every bus has been in by 01:30.

blocks.label: depot_night_0100_0310.png

diagram.aria: Friday 16 October 01:00 to 03:10. The 38 buses that came in by 00:50 are checked in the whole time. The 7 diverted buses of routes 7 and 12 are on the diversion until 02:20, then checked in. Route 4's rows in the warehouse: none until 02:00, 952 from the 02:00 run, 1,904 from the 02:40 run. Markers: 02:00 the job runs; 02:20 the 7 buses come in; 02:40 the job runs again; 03:05 the report preview.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the check-in lines on my screen and the job's run times, Friday 16 October 01:00 to 03:10. Green is checked in: the 38 were all in by 00:50, the 7 diverted buses at 02:20. Route 4's rows in the warehouse: 952 after the 02:00 run (green), 1,904 after the 02:40 run (red), against bus 17's slip of 952.

blocks.text: At 03:05 the report preview popped up on my screen, as it does after every run. Each line: route, buses, passengers on the report.

route 4      1 bus      1,904
route 7      4 buses    2,610
route 12     3 buses    1,734
the rest    37 buses   60,808
all         45 buses   67,056
Twice the slip, to the ticket. As if bus 17 had come home twice.
The claim goes to the council at 08:00 on Friday. The day manager reads my handover at 07:00, and the job belongs to head office, not to me. What should we change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Your job is a batch: it gathers a whole night of tickets and handles them in one go. Before you blame the total, sort the routes. Which ones are right, which are doubled, and when did each of those buses check in, before 02:00 or after? Then ask the data team one thing: when a second run finds rows a first run already loaded, what does it do with them?

replies.author: u/depot_tray_jozef
replies.text: Routes 7 and 12 match their slips to the ticket. Every bus that was in by 02:00 is exactly doubled. The data team's line opens at 08:00.

comments.author: u/four_am_seydou
comments.text: You're overthinking it. Move the job to 04:00. No bus has ever come in later than that; even tonight's diversion had them home by 02:20. One run, after everyone's in, and nobody ever has to press run again.

replies.author: u/depot_tray_jozef
replies.text: That's one number in head office's timer. They could change it this morning.

comments.author: u/every_fare_yaroslava
comments.text: Why wait for the night at all? Send each fare live: the moment a ticket is sold, the machine sends it over the phone network, like a card payment, and the depot adds it to the count as it arrives. A flow of single fares like that is called a stream, a river where your nightly job is a lake. No nightly job, nothing to run twice.

replies.author: u/depot_tray_jozef
replies.text: Route 12's diversion runs through the old railway cutting. Phones get no signal down there.

reply.prompt: The day manager reads the handover at 07:00 on Friday and calls head office. What should they change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Move the nightly job from 02:00 to 04:00, so every late bus is in before it runs.
options.verdict: Still a guess at the clock
options.part2: Head office moved the timer to 04:00 that morning, and Tolulope in the data team cleared the night's rows and ran the job once more by hand, so the 08:00 claim went out at 35,700. Until November the 04:00 run matched every slip. Then on the night of Tuesday 3 November, route 12's bus 43 lost a wheel on the moor road and was towed in at 04:20, after the job had run without it. I followed the runbook at 04:40. In the sim, replaying 15 October with bus 43 held until 04:20: the 04:00 run claims 35,122, without its 578 tickets, and the re-run at 04:40 adds all 45 files on top: 70,822, and route 4 shows 1,904 again.
options.senior: Moving the timer guesses a later time instead of an earlier one; the job still starts when a clock rings, not when the night's data is complete. It works until the first bus later than the guess, and then the old problem returns in full, because each run still adds rows: a missed bus means a re-run, and a re-run doubles everyone already loaded. Start the job on the evidence that the data is in, and make a run safe to repeat.

options.text: Send each fare to the depot live as it is sold, and count it the moment it arrives.
options.part2: Head office cleared the night's rows and ran the job once more by hand for the 08:00 claim, then spent November fitting every machine to send each fare over the phone network and building a system that counts fares all day. In the sim, replaying 15 October with live fares: at 01:00 the count already reads 35,582 and route 4 shows 952, with no nightly job and nothing to run twice. But route 12 sold 118 fares in the railway cutting, where there is no signal; they waited in the machines until the buses docked at 02:20 and resent them, and only then did the count reach 35,700. The phone bill for 45 machines, a system that must run every hour of every day, and a rule for when the count for a night is closed are now head office's to run.
options.senior: This is an honest design: a stream is fresh all day and has no nightly job to run twice. But it does not remove late data, it renames it. A fare sold where there is no signal arrives hours after it happened, so the stream still needs a rule for how long a night stays open and what to do with fares that come after. It also needs signal on every bus and a system running all day. For a claim the council reads once a day, a batch that waits for its data is usually simpler and cheaper; a stream earns its cost when someone needs the answer within minutes.

options.text: Never run the job twice in one night, so no bus can have its fares counted twice.
options.part2: Head office crossed the late-bus page out of the runbook, then cleared the night's rows and ran the job once more by hand for the 08:00 claim. Nothing was counted twice again. But on any night a bus comes in after 02:00, its tickets now never reach the report. In the sim, replaying 15 October with no re-run: the 02:00 run counts the 38 buses already in, route 4 shows 952, and the 7 diverted buses' 4,344 tickets never arrive: 31,356 claimed against 35,700 on the slips.
options.senior: Forbidding the re-run swaps one wrong answer for another: no doubles, but every late bus is left out, and the council pays for fewer passengers than rode. The re-run was never the fault; a re-run that adds instead of replacing is. Late data will keep coming, so the job needs a way to take it in safely, not a rule that pretends it won't.

options.text: Wait for every bus to check in, and let each run replace that night's rows.
options.part2: Tolulope came in at 06:30, switched the load back to replacing the night's rows and ran tonight's job once: 35,700, route 4 952, and the claim went at 08:00. By Monday 19 October the job started when all 45 buses had checked in, not at 02:00. If a bus is still out at 04:00, the cut-off, the job runs anyway and the report goes with the missing bus marked; when its file lands later, the job runs again for that night. Each run deletes the night's rows and loads every file again, so a second run gives the same answer. The raw files stay in the lake, which is all the council's dispute ever needed. In the sim, replaying 15 October: the job starts at 02:20, when the last bus checks in: 35,700, route 4 952. With bus 43 held until 04:20: 35,122 at 04:00 with bus 43 marked, then 35,700 at 04:20. I rewrote the runbook's late-bus page with the data team: there is nothing to press now.
options.senior: A scheduled job should start when its data is complete, not when a clock rings: here, when all 45 buses have checked in, with a stated cut-off and a rule for files that come after it. And every run should rebuild its night's slice from scratch, so running it again, by a person, a late file or a retry, can only make the answer right, never bigger. Keep history in the raw files, not by stacking loads in the report's table.

sim.title: Replay the night at the Burnhollow depot
sim.lede: You're Jozef at 01:00 on Friday 16 October, replaying the night to 05:00 in 10-minute steps. As given data: 45 buses, and one ticket is one passenger. Route 4's only bus, 17, docked at 23:40 with 952 tickets. 38 buses were in by 00:50: bus 17 and 37 others with 30,404 tickets, 31,356 in all. Route 7's four buses (2,610 tickets) and route 12's three (578 each, 1,734) dock at 02:20. All 45 slips: 35,700. As built, the nightly job starts at 02:00 by the clock and adds rows, and the clerk runs it again 20 minutes after late buses dock, as the runbook says. With live fares, route 12 sold 118 fares in the cutting with no signal (40, 39 and 39 on buses 41, 42 and 43); each machine resends its share when its bus docks. You can also hold bus 43 until 04:20, or break its machine so it never checks in. Set when the job starts, whether each run adds rows or replaces the night's rows (its slice of the table), the clerk's re-run and live fares, then step or play to 05:00.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play it as built: route 4 shows 1,904 and the report 67,056, with 31,356 fares counted twice. Switch the load to replace the night's slice: 952 and 35,700. Turn the re-run off instead: 31,356, with 7 buses missing. Start at 04:00: one run, 35,700; now hold bus 43 until 04:20: 35,122 at 04:00, then 70,822 after the 04:40 re-run. Start when all 45 have checked in: 02:20, 35,700; break bus 43's machine and there is no report by 05:00. Try a 04:00 cut-off (run anyway at 04:00, with missing buses marked) and a late-file rule (a file that lands after a run starts the job again), with replace. Turn on live fares: 35,582 at 01:00, 35,700 once route 12 docks.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at the depot broke. In head office's building, three weeks ago, the nightly job was changed from replacing the night's rows to adding them, and the runbook, written for the old way, told the clerk to run it again. The 38 buses already loaded were loaded twice: route 4's 952 became 1,904.

steps.title: A bus's day, from ticket machine to lake.
steps.text: Each bus's tickets reach head office in four steps. First, the bus docks on its bay and its ticket machine joins the depot's wifi. Second, the machine sends the day's tickets as one file into the lake, a store that keeps raw files exactly as they came. Third, when the whole file is in, the machine reports that the bus has checked in, with its count: bus 17, 952 tickets, at 23:40. Fourth, the driver prints the end-of-day slip with the same count. What can go wrong: a bus held on a diversion docks late, as routes 7 and 12 did at 02:20; a machine that cannot reach the wifi sends nothing; and a lake keeps whatever arrives, so on its own it never says whether tonight's files are all there. Only the check-ins say that.

steps.title: The 02:00 job: a batch, cleaned then loaded, started by the clock.
steps.text: A batch gathers a whole night of data and handles it in one go; a stream handles each fare as it arrives, a river where the batch is a lake (s4e04). The depot's job is a batch, and cron, a timer, starts it at 02:00 whatever has arrived. Then it works in four steps: it reads every file in tonight's part of the lake; it cleans each file into rows, one per ticket; it loads the rows into the warehouse, the tidy tables for reports; and it counts each route's rows into the morning report. Cleaning before loading is called ETL, short for extract, transform, load. The other order, ELT (extract, load, transform), loads the raw rows first and cleans them inside the warehouse with its own tools, which suits warehouses with plenty of computing power. Either order has the same weak point here: a clock decides when the night's data is complete, and a clock cannot know.

steps.title: Add rows, then run again: 952 became 1,904.
steps.text: On Thursday 24 September, after the council disputed August's claim, Tolulope in head office's data team changed how the job loads. Before, each run replaced tonight's rows: it deleted them and loaded every file again, so a second run gave the same answer. After, each run added its rows on top, so every load was kept as its own set. The runbook's late-bus page was written for the old way, and nobody connected the two. Tonight, the 02:00 run loaded the 38 buses already in: 31,356 tickets, route 4's 952 among them. The 02:40 run added all 45 files, 35,700 tickets, on top. 31,356 + 35,700 = 67,056 on the report; route 4, 952 + 952 = 1,904; routes 7 and 12, loaded once, matched their slips. For three weeks every bus had been in by 01:30, so nobody pressed run again, and the change waited for the first late night.

steps.title: The fix: start on data, not the clock, and let each run replace its night.
steps.text: Running on data means the job starts when the night's data is complete, not when a timer rings. First, the scheduler, the program that starts jobs, watches the check-ins. Second, when all 45 buses have checked in, it starts the job. Third, if a bus is still out at a stated cut-off, 04:00, it starts anyway and the report goes with the missing bus marked. Fourth, the late-file rule from the sim: when a file lands after a run, the job runs again for that night. Each run deletes the night's slice, its rows for that one night, and loads every file again as one step, so a second run gives the same rows: the run is idempotent, safe to repeat. History lives in the lake, which keeps every raw file, so nothing needs to be added twice to keep it. In the sim tonight, the job starts at 02:20: 35,700, route 4 952; run it again and nothing changes. If the scheduler runs on two or more computers so it survives one breaking, it must still start each job once, by holding a lock, as the bell tower's controllers had to in "The Lock Nobody Holds" (s8e08). What can still go wrong: a machine that never checks in holds the report until the cut-off.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fail, and the walk into the other building.
steps.text: Moving the job to 04:00 works tonight, 35,700, but it is still a guess at the clock: in the sim, with bus 43 held until 04:20, the 04:00 run misses its 578 tickets, and the runbook re-run at 04:40 doubles every other bus again, 70,822. Never running twice leaves the 7 diverted buses out: 31,356 claimed for 35,700 passengers. Sending every fare live, a stream, is fresh all day, but it needs signal on every bus and a system running all day, and the 118 fares route 12 sold in the cutting wait in the machines until the buses dock; late fares still need rules, which "Counting Clicks", later this season, is about. A bigger warehouse loads the same rows twice, only faster. At 06:30 Jozef put bus 17's slip in his pocket and crossed the yard to head office, into the building where the night began. Tolulope opened the job's settings beside him, and there it was, three weeks old: load mode, add rows.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for one night. The 45 ticket machines send one file each into the lake and report each check-in. The check-in list reaches 45 of 45, or the 04:00 cut-off passes. The scheduler then starts the job once. The job reads the lake and replaces tonight's slice in the warehouse. The warehouse counts the morning report: 35,700, route 4 952.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for one night. The job starts when the check-in list reaches 45 of 45, or at the 04:00 cut-off with the missing buses marked, and the scheduler starts it once. Each run replaces tonight's slice of the warehouse from the files in the lake, so a second run gives the same 35,700 and route 4 stays at 952.

fix.title: The fix: start when all 45 have checked in, cut off at 04:00, and replace the night's slice each run
fix.text: Write down what makes a night complete: all 45 buses checked in. Have the scheduler start the job on that, not at a clock time, with a stated cut-off at 04:00 when the job runs anyway and the report marks any missing bus, and a late-file rule that runs the job again for that night when a file lands after a run. Make every run delete the night's slice and load every file again as one step, so a run repeated by a person, a late file or a retry gives the same rows. Keep history in the lake's raw files, not by adding loads to the report's table. Run the scheduler so that each job starts once even across several computers. And when anyone changes how a job loads, read every runbook page that tells someone to run it.

limits: Waiting for check-ins trusts the machines. A machine that breaks and never checks in holds the report until the 04:00 cut-off, and then the report goes short: in the sim, 35,122 with bus 43 marked missing, its 578 tickets on its slip only until the machine is fixed.

Replacing the night's slice is safe only if the delete and the load happen as one step and only one run happens at a time. Two schedulers starting the same job together can still load a night twice; one runner per job matters as much as the replace.

A file that lands after the 08:00 claim has gone means a corrected claim. The cut-off and the late-file rule need a written answer to how late a correction may still go to the council, and who sends it.

head: What head office does
Good
Bad
rows: 02:00 by the clock, add rows, runbook re-run (as now)
Bus 43 held to 04:20: 35,122, or 70,822 after the runbook re-run.
118 fares wait until docking; signal on every bus, a system all day, rules for late fares.
Wait for 45 check-ins, 04:00 cut-off, replace the night's slice (the fix)
A missing bus holds the report to 04:00, then it goes marked short.

explain.seniorTake: A scheduled job is a promise about data, not about time. Write down what a complete night means, here 45 check-ins, and start on that, with a cut-off for the night it never happens and a rule for files that come after. Then make every run safe to repeat: each run rebuilds one night's slice in one step, so a re-run, a late file or a nervous clerk can only make the answer right, never bigger. Keep history in the lake, raw and dated, not by stacking loads in the report's table. Choose batch or stream by how fresh the answer must be: a claim read once a day is usually batch work, and a stream brings its own late data. Make sure the scheduler starts each job once, however many computers it runs on. And when you change how a job loads, read every runbook page that tells someone to run it.

realWorld.title: Airflow: a run waits for its interval to end
realWorld.text: Apache Airflow is a widely used scheduler for data jobs. A Dag is its name for a job made of steps, and its guide to Dag runs says that "A Dag run is usually scheduled after its associated data interval has ended", so that the run has all the data for its period. The data interval is the stretch of time a run covers: at the depot, one night of tickets.

realWorld.title: Airflow: runs for missed and past intervals
realWorld.text: When the scheduler has missed intervals, Airflow can start a run for each one: "This concept is called Catchup." Running a job over a stretch of the past on purpose has its own name: "This process is known as Backfill." Both are usually safe only when a run for one interval can be repeated without adding to what an earlier run loaded: the replace-the-slice rule.

realWorld.title: Spark: an engine for large jobs
realWorld.text: Apache Spark's documentation opens: "Apache Spark is a unified analytics engine for large-scale data processing." Engines like it are often used for batch work such as the depot's nightly load, run over a night's or a month's files at once.

realWorld.title: Spark: a stream treated like a batch
realWorld.text: Spark's streaming guide treats a stream as a table that keeps growing, so the same kind of query works on both: "This leads to a new stream processing model that is very similar to a batch processing model." Batch and stream differ in when the answer is ready, more than in what the answer is.

realWorld.title: Flink: two clocks for every fare
realWorld.text: Apache Flink, a stream engine, separates two times. "Event time is the time that each individual event occurred on its producing device." And: "Processing time refers to the system time of the machine that is executing the respective operation." A fare sold in the cutting and resent at 02:20 has its event time in the evening and its processing time at 02:20.

realWorld.title: Flink: streams expect late data
realWorld.text: Flink tracks how far a stream has got in event time with watermarks: "The mechanism in Flink to measure progress in event time is watermarks." Some data still arrives after the watermark has passed it: "For this reason, streaming programs may explicitly expect some late elements." A stream does not remove the depot's late-bus problem; it gives it a new name.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001 A.5.37: procedures that keep up
realWorld.text: ISMS.online's guide to Annex A control 5.37, documented operating procedures, says: "The approaches above should be subject to periodic and/or ad-hoc reviews as and when required." The depot's runbook page was right for replace and wrong for add, and nothing tied a change to the job to a review of the page.

asked: Batch or stream for this report?
How do you make a re-run of a data job safe?
How would you build a scheduler that runs each job once across many machines?
interview.answer: I'd start from who reads the answer and when. The council reads one claim a day, so a batch that runs once a night is usually enough and cheaper to run; a stream earns its cost when someone needs the answer within minutes, and it still needs rules for late data, because a fare sold with no signal arrives hours late. ETL cleans the data before loading it into the warehouse; ELT loads the raw data first and cleans it inside the warehouse with the warehouse's own tools. ELT keeps the raw rows to hand for re-cleaning later and suits warehouses with plenty of computing power, such as Snowflake-style ones rented as a service; ETL keeps the warehouse tidy and its cost down. Either way the raw files stay in the lake. To make a re-run safe I'd make each run idempotent: it owns one slice, one night, and replaces that slice in one step, deleting and loading inside one transaction or loading into a fresh copy and swapping it in. Then a retry, a late file or a person pressing run again can only make the answer right. I'd also start it on data, not the clock: when every source has checked in, with a stated cut-off and a late-file rule. For a scheduler on many machines, I'd keep the schedule and each run's state in one shared store that the machines agree on, and have a machine take a lock or a lease with a fencing token before it starts a run, so only one starts each job, and the idempotent run covers the rare case where two still do. I'd tell the story of a bus depot whose job changed from replacing rows to adding them, where the runbook's re-run turned route 4's 952 passengers into 1,904.

terms.def: The yard and building where a bus company's buses park overnight. Burnhollow Buses has 45.
The person at the depot counter overnight who takes in slips, watches the check-ins and follows the runbook. Jozef works 22:00 to 06:00.
The bill the bus company sends the council each morning. The council pays a set amount per passenger, and one ticket is one passenger.
The machine on each bus that sells and records tickets. When the bus docks, it sends the day's tickets as one file to the lake.
Park a bus on its bay for the night, where its ticket machine joins the depot's wifi and sends its file.
One saved bundle of data with a name, like a document on a phone. Each bus sends one file a night with all its tickets.
A store that keeps raw files exactly as they came, cheaply and for a long time, like a sack of unopened post. Burnhollow's lake is on head office's computers.
Files kept as they arrived, before any cleaning or sorting. The lake keeps them, so a night can always be loaded again.
A bus's ticket machine reporting that its whole file is in the lake, with its count: "bus 17 checked in, 952 tickets". The signal that a bus's data is complete.
A printed slip from the ticket machine with the day's ticket count, which the driver drops in the clerk's tray.
A set of instructions a computer carries out once a night, here to load the night's files into the warehouse and build the morning report.
A timer on a computer that starts a job at set times, like an alarm clock: "run at 02:00 every day". It does not check whether the data is there.
The program that decides when each job starts: by the clock, like cron, or when its data is ready. A careful one starts each job once, even across several computers.
One line in a table, here one ticket: route, bus, time and fare. The report counts rows.
Data laid out in rows and columns, like a spreadsheet. The warehouse keeps the tickets in tables.
A store of tidy tables built for reports and questions, filled from cleaned data. Burnhollow's morning report is counted from it.
The count of passengers per route that the nightly job builds from the warehouse, used for the 08:00 claim.
The screen at the depot counter that shows the morning report as soon as each run finishes. It alerted Jozef at 03:05.
A binder or page of steps to follow when something happens, written so anyone on shift can follow it. Burnhollow's late-bus page says to run the job again.
Running a job again over the same night: it reads every file in tonight's part of the lake again and loads the rows. Safe only if it replaces, not adds.
How a job puts rows into the warehouse: adding them on top of what is there, or replacing the night's rows.
A load mode that puts each run's rows on top of what is already there. Run twice, it counts everything twice.
The part of a table that belongs to one stretch of time, here one night's rows. Replacing a slice deletes those rows and loads them fresh.
A load mode that deletes the night's rows and loads every file again as one step, so a second run gives the same rows.
A job that gathers a whole stretch of data, such as one night's tickets, and handles it in one go. The depot's nightly job is one.
Data handled one piece at a time as it arrives, like a river, instead of gathered into a lake first (s4e04).
Each fare sent over the phone network the moment it is sold, and counted as it arrives, like a card payment.
The radio link a phone or ticket machine needs to send data over the phone network. The railway cutting on route 12's diversion has none, so live fares sold there wait.
A deep trench dug for a railway, often with steep sides. Route 12's diversion runs through an old one with no phone signal.
Extract, transform, load: take the data out of its source, clean it, then load the tidy rows into the warehouse. The depot's job works this way.
Extract, load, transform: load the raw data into the warehouse first, then clean it there with the warehouse's own tools.
Turn raw data into tidy rows: split it into lines, fix the layout, drop what is broken. The transform step of ETL and ELT.
Starting a job when its data is complete, such as when all 45 buses have checked in, instead of at a clock time.
A stated time when a job runs anyway, even if some data is missing, and marks what is missing. 04:00 in the fix.
A rule that a file landing after a run starts the job again for that night, so the late data is taken in.
Safe to repeat: doing it twice leaves the same result as doing it once. A run that replaces its night's slice is idempotent (s4e07).
A group of changes a database makes as one step: all of them happen, or none do. Deleting and loading a night inside one makes the replace safe.
A permission only one holder may have at a time, like the single key to a room (s8e08). A scheduler on several computers holds one before starting a job.
A lock that runs out after a set time unless renewed, so a computer that dies does not hold it for ever.
A number handed out with each lock, one higher each time, so a late holder's work can be refused (s8e08).
The bus company's office building across the depot yard, where the data team and the computers that run the job are.
The people at head office who build and run the lake, the warehouse and the nightly job. Tolulope is one of them.
A longer route a bus is sent on when its usual road is shut. Routes 7 and 12 were diverted at 23:15.
Free software widely used to schedule data jobs made of steps, decide when each run starts and keep a record of every run.
Airflow's name for a job made of steps, each step pointing to the ones that follow it. Short for directed acyclic graph.
In Airflow, the stretch of time a run covers, such as one night. A run usually starts after its interval has ended.
In Airflow, starting a run for every interval the scheduler missed, one after another.
Running a job on purpose over a stretch of the past, for example to rebuild last month's tables.
Free software for processing large amounts of data across many computers, often used for batch jobs.
Free software for processing streams, one event at a time, with care for when each event really happened.
When something really happened, such as the moment a fare was sold, as recorded by the device.
When a computer handles something, which can be hours after it happened, such as a fare resent at 02:20.
A stream engine's marker of how far it has got in event time: up to here, we think everything has arrived.
Data that arrives after the job or stream has moved past its time, like a bus that docks after the run.
A kind of data warehouse rented as a service over the internet, with computing power that can grow for big jobs.
An audit report, by outside checkers, on how a company controls its systems, judged against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria.
The SOC 2 area about processing being complete, valid, accurate and on time. For the depot: each fare counted once, none left out.
An international standard for running information security. Its Annex A lists controls, among them A.5.37 on documented operating procedures.
The control on documented operating procedures: write down how systems are run, make the steps available, and keep them up to date as things change.

atWork: Look for any scheduled data job that starts at a clock time and has a written instruction to run it again when data comes in late. Then check one thing: what does a second run do with rows the first run loaded? A nightly load that was changed from replacing its night to adding rows, without anyone changing the re-run instructions, is a common pattern, and it stays hidden until the first night someone follows them. For each job: write down what makes its data complete (every source checked in, every file present) and start on that, with a stated cut-off and a late-file rule; make each run rebuild its own slice in one step, so it is safe to repeat; keep raw files for history instead of stacking loads; and if the scheduler runs on several machines, make sure each job starts once. Tie every change to a job's load to a review of the runbook pages that tell people to run it. Standards: if your company is pursuing SOC 2 with the processing integrity criteria (PI1), an auditor would look for evidence that processing is complete and accurate, here that each fare is counted once and none is left out, such as a nightly check of the report against the slips. If it is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.5.37 (documented operating procedures) expects procedures that are kept up to date; ISMS.online's explainer says they "should be subject to periodic and/or ad-hoc reviews as and when required". Build the check and the runbook review in from the first draft rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your team runs a job at 03:00 that loads each shop's till files from a store of raw files into the sales tables, then builds the regional sales report. Last month someone changed the load so it keeps every load's rows instead of overwriting them. Tonight two shops' files arrived at 03:30, so the night manager ran the job again at 04:00, as the run sheet says. The report shows every other shop's sales doubled. What happened, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The second run put the same night's rows on top of the first run's, so every shop already loaded was counted again
Make each run replace that night's slice in one step, so running it again gives the same answer (idempotent)
Start the job when every shop's file is in (or at a stated cut-off with a late-file rule), not at a clock time

recall.model: The second run put the same night's rows on top of the first run's: every shop that was already in was loaded twice, which is why their sales doubled and the two late shops look right. The re-run instruction was written for a load that replaced; nobody changed it when the load started keeping every set. I'd make each run replace that night's slice in one step, deleting and reloading inside one transaction, so running it again gives the same answer: the run is idempotent. History stays in the raw files. And I'd start the job on data, not the clock: wait for every shop's file to be in, with a stated cut-off and a late-file rule that rebuilds the night when a file comes after.

recall.prompt: With the load set to add rows, the 02:00 run loaded the 38 buses already in (31,356 tickets) and the 02:40 run loaded all 45 files (35,700 tickets). What did the morning report claim in all?
recall.why: Adding rows keeps both runs: 31,356 + 35,700 = 67,056. 35,700 is what a run that replaces the night's slice gives. 62,712 doubles only the 38 early buses and forgets the 7 late ones; 71,400 doubles all 45, but the late buses were loaded once.

options: Clean the files first, then load the tidy rows into the warehouse
Load the raw data into the warehouse first, then clean it there with the warehouse's own tools
Send each fare live and count it the moment it arrives
Keep the raw files in the lake and never load them anywhere
recall.why: ELT is extract, load, transform: the raw data goes into the warehouse first and is cleaned inside it. Cleaning first and loading after is ETL, the depot's job. Counting each fare as it arrives is a stream, and a lake on its own is storage, not a way of loading.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: batch or stream for a report a council receives once each morning? What would make you change your answer?

keyIdeas.idea: A batch is enough for a daily deadline, and usually simpler and cheaper to run
A stream earns its cost when someone needs the answer within minutes
Either way, late data needs a rule: a cut-off, event time or watermarks

recall.model: For a report read once each morning, a batch is usually enough: one run a night, after the data is in, is simpler and cheaper than a system running all day. I'd change my answer if someone needed the figures within minutes, say a control room watching crowds as it happens; then a stream earns its cost. Either way late data needs a rule: a batch needs a cut-off and a late-file rule, and a stream needs event time and watermarks to decide when a period is closed and what to do with what arrives after.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 2 months later. Since Monday 19 October the job has started when all 45 buses check in, with the 04:00 cut-off, and each run deletes the night's rows and then loads every file. Every claim has matched the slips. On Monday 30 November head office added a second computer running the scheduler, so the job still starts if one computer breaks. On the night of Wednesday 9 December the last bus checked in at 01:10, and both computers started the job within the same second. The morning report said route 4 carried 1,902 passengers; bus 17's slip said 951.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did a job that deletes before it loads still count bus 17 twice, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: Two runs at once interleaved: both deleted the night's rows, then both loaded, because the delete and the load were separate steps
Only one runner per job: the schedulers must take a lock or lease before starting, so the second stands by (s8e08)
Make the replace a single step, a transaction or a swap of a fresh copy, so even two runs leave one copy

coldCase.model: The replace was two separate steps, and two runs interleaved. Both schedulers started at once: each deleted the night's rows before either had loaded anything, then each loaded every file. So bus 17's 951 tickets went in twice: 1,902. Two fixes, and they belong together. Only one runner per job: the two schedulers must take a lock or lease before starting a night's job, with a fencing token so a late holder is refused, as in "The Lock Nobody Holds", and the second stands by. And make the replace a single step: delete and load inside one transaction, or load into a fresh copy and swap it in, all or nothing, so even if two runs ever start, the night ends with one copy.
